discovery: Optical detection and coherent control of single spins in diamond and their development into nanoscale quantum sensors
motivation: Wrachtrup and co-workers first detected the magnetic resonance of a single nitrogen-vacancy spin in diamond by optical means (1997). They then achieved room-temperature coherent control of the spin and coupling to nearby nuclear spins. In 2008 Lukin, Walsworth and Wrachtrup proposed and demonstrated that a single spin can serve as an atomic-scale magnetometer whose readout is limited only by quantum projection noise. Their work turned a fundamental single-quantum-system experiment into a measurement tool that works at room temperature and in many environments. NV sensors now image magnetism in two-dimensional materials and superconductors, current flow in devices, magnetic fields from neurons and living cells, and the magnetic properties of samples above 100 GPa inside diamond anvil cells. Few quantum technologies have given so many fields of physics, from condensed matter and geoscience to biology, such a new and reliable way to measure.
